summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Appeals Court affirmed a termination decree over an Indian Child Welfare Act challenge, holding that the department satisfied 25 U.S.C. § 1912(a) notice where the three federally recognized Cherokee tribes responded that the child was not an "Indian child," and rejecting the related reasonable-efforts and unfitness claims.
key_cases.relevance: Uday is the only Massachusetts appellate decision located that reaches an ICWA issue, and it governs the department's notice obligation when a child may have tribal ancestry.
key_cases.quote: These responsive letters from the three Cherokee tribes demonstrate that the department in fact did comply with ICWA notice provision.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court rejected all challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act, holding that Congress had authority to enact it, that its placement preferences and active-efforts provisions do not violate the anticommandeering doctrine, and that the equal protection and nondelegation claims failed for lack of standing.
key_cases.relevance: Brackeen confirms that ICWA's jurisdictional, active-efforts and placement-preference requirements bind Massachusetts state courts in any proceeding involving an Indian child.
key_cases.quote: we reject all of petitioners’ challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

search_keywords: Massachusetts Department of Children and Families

state_agency.name: Massachusetts Department of Children and Families
state_agency.hotline: 1-800-792-5200 (Massachusetts Child Abuse Emergency Line, for nights, weekends and holidays; weekdays 8:45 a.m. to 5 p.m. call the DCF area office for the city or town where the child lives)

mandatory_reporters: Medical and mental health professionals — physician, medical intern, hospital personnel engaged in the examination, care or treatment of persons, medical examiner, psychologist, emergency medical technician, dentist, nurse, chiropractor, podiatrist, optometrist, osteopath, allied mental health and human services professional licensed under M.G.L. c. 112, § 165, drug and alcoholism counselor, psychiatrist, clinical social worker — M.G.L. c. 119, § 21 (definition of "mandated reporter"), cl. (i)

School and child care personnel — public or private school teacher, educational administrator, guidance or family counselor, child care worker, person paid to care for or work with a child in any public or private facility, home or program funded by the Commonwealth or licensed under M.G.L. c. 15D, licensor of the Department of Early Education and Care, school attendance officer — M.G.L. c. 119, § 21, cl. (ii)

Justice-system, public-safety and placement personnel — probation officer, clerk-magistrate of a district court, parole officer, social worker, foster parent, firefighter, police officer, animal control officer — M.G.L. c. 119, § 21, cl. (iii)

Clergy and religious personnel — priest, rabbi, clergy member, ordained or licensed minister, leader of any church or religious body, accredited Christian Science practitioner, person performing official duties on behalf of a church or religious body, or person employed by a church or religious body to supervise, educate, coach, train or counsel a child on a regular basis; information gained solely in a confession or similarly confidential religious communication need not be reported (M.G.L. c. 119, § 51A(j)) — M.G.L. c. 119, § 21, cl. (iv)
Any person in charge of a medical or other public or private institution, school or facility, or that person's designated agent — M.G.L. c. 119, § 21, cl. (v)
The Child Advocate — M.G.L. c. 119, § 21, cl. (vi)
Massachusetts is not a universal-reporting state: any person MAY file a report, but only mandated reporters must — M.G.L. c. 119, § 51A(a) and (f)

timeline_requirements.deadline: 2 hours to begin an emergency response; 2 business days to begin a non-emergency response
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Initial contact on a screened-in 51A report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No penalty stated in M.G.L. c. 119, § 51B; the non-emergency timeframe may be extended only by a waiver approved by the DCF area director or requested by law enforcement (§ 51B(d))

timeline_requirements.deadline: 5 business days for the final report on an emergency response; 15 business days for the determination on a non-emergency response
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Initial contact on a screened-in 51A report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No penalty stated in M.G.L. c. 119, § 51B; the 15-business-day determination may be extended only by a waiver approved by the DCF area director or requested by law enforcement (§ 51B(d))
